prerequisites: It is recommended that students have passed the 2nd year course “Materials Science”.

learning_outcomes.text: Calculate the integrity of cracked industrial components under mechanical service loads.
Calculate the life of industrial components under fatigue loads and combinations of static load/corrosive environment, and also to assess the influence of influencing factors.
Predict the behavior of materials in situations of creep, oxidation, and hot corrosion, and select the most suitable materials for each particular case.
Predict the behavior of materials in situations of friction/wear, and select the most suitable materials for each particular case.
Define the suitable surface modification technology to withstand different service actions.

syllabus_topics: Fundamental mechanical properties: Tensile, compression and flexural tests. Behavior of metallic alloys, ceramics and plastic materials. Tests on notched specimens.
Toughness: Definition of impact toughness. Charpy tests. Ductile-brittle transition curve and transition temperature. Factors influencing brittleness. Other tests for measuring toughness.
Micromechanisms of fracture: Microstructure. Hardening mechanisms. Ductile, brittle and intergranular fracture. Microstructural modifications for increasing material toughness.
Linear elastic fracture mechanics: Energy criterion for fracture. Stress state ahead of a crack. Stress intensity factor. Fracture toughness. Plane stress versus plane strain.
Elastoplastic fracture mechanics: CTOD and J-integral. Fracture criteria. Experimental determination of material toughness. Limitations of elastoplastic fracture mechanics.
Fatigue: Load cycles. Justifying mechanisms for fatigue cracking. Descriptive laws. Fatigue limit. Standardized tests. Threshold value and fatigue crack growth rate. Calculation of fatigue lives.
Environmentally assisted fracture: Justifying mechanisms. Descriptive laws. Standardized tests. Threshold value and growth rate of environmentally assisted cracks. Calculation of service lives.
Creep: Evolution of deformation as a function of time. Descriptive laws of creep. Stress relaxation at high temperature. Creep deformation mechanisms. Deformation maps.
Oxidation and hot corrosion. Justifying mechanisms of these processes. Reaction kinetics and behavior laws. Development of high-temperature resistant materials. Hot corrosion.

Wet corrosion. Thermodynamics and kinetics of corrosive processes. Electrode potentials and galvanic cells. Justifying mechanisms. Passivation. Corrosion morphologies. Methods for controlling corrosive processes. Electrochemical protection.
Friction and wear of materials. Surface contact. Adhesive, abrasive and fatigue wear. Tests.
Surface protection technologies. Surface treatments. Coatings and application methods. Comparison of available processes
assessment_rules: The final grade is calculated as: 0.1*PLs + 0.1*EP1 + 0.1*EP2 + 0.04*EO1 + 0.04*EO2 + 0.62*EF. To pass, a minimum overall score of 5 out of 10 points is required. The Final Exam (EF) requires a minimum of 4 points out of 10, with at least 30% in both the exercises and theoretical parts. Mandatory submission of proposed exercises and at least 85% attendance at Laboratory Practices are required for ordinary assessment. In the extraordinary assessment, notes from PLs, EP1, EP2, EO1-PL13, and EO2-TG are carried over, and the Final Exam (EF) evaluates the entire syllabus with the same minimum requirements.
